items.prompt: "Illegal states unrepresentable" means:
choices: Shaping types/interfaces so an invalid combination of data cannot be constructed at all, not just checked after the fact
Writing enough runtime validation that every invalid input gets a clear error message
Adding comments to a function explaining which argument combinations are unsafe
Rejecting any API design that uses optional parameters
items.explanation: The phrase is specifically about the type/interface itself excluding invalid shapes — a validation function that runs and throws is still allowing the invalid shape to be constructed in the first place; illegal-states-unrepresentable means that construction step fails, usually at compile time.
items.reference:
🚫 Illegal state — channel: 'sms' with no phoneNumber
🧱 Made unrepresentable — the type for an sms channel has no shape without a phoneNumber field

Why: a state that can't be constructed can't reach production, no matter how many code paths exist.
items.learnMore: Illegal-states-unrepresentable is a design goal, not a single technique — the most common tool for reaching it in a typed language is a discriminated union (see L2/L3), where each tagged shape only carries the fields valid for that tag. The alternative — a single type with every field optional and a comment saying which combinations are meaningless — leaves the invalid combination fully constructible; every reader and every future contributor has to independently remember the rule the comment states, forever, and Alertly's outage is exactly what happens when one of them doesn't.

items.prompt: Alertly's SendAlertOptions type had emailAddress, phoneNumber, and deviceToken all marked optional, regardless of which channel was chosen. What does this represent, in terms of illegal states?
choices: It's a convenience — callers only need to fill in the field they care about
It's exactly the problem: the type can represent channel: 'sms' with none of the three fields set, a state that should be impossible
It's fine because the compiler still checks the field types are strings
It's only a problem if the fields are also renamed inconsistently
items.explanation: Making every channel-specific field optional on every call means the type allows combinations that are never actually valid for any given channel — the type is more permissive than the real, valid domain of the data, which is the definition of the type leaving an illegal state representable.
items.reference:
🚫 Illegal state — channel: 'sms' with no phoneNumber
🧱 Made unrepresentable — the type for an sms channel has no shape without a phoneNumber field

Why: a state that can't be constructed can't reach production, no matter how many code paths exist.
items.learnMore: Illegal-states-unrepresentable is a design goal, not a single technique — the most common tool for reaching it in a typed language is a discriminated union (see L2/L3), where each tagged shape only carries the fields valid for that tag. The alternative — a single type with every field optional and a comment saying which combinations are meaningless — leaves the invalid combination fully constructible; every reader and every future contributor has to independently remember the rule the comment states, forever, and Alertly's outage is exactly what happens when one of them doesn't.

items.prompt: A colleague says: "We already handle this — there's an if-check deep in the SMS client that throws if phoneNumber is missing." Why doesn't that alone satisfy "illegal states unrepresentable"?
choices: Because the check still allows the invalid SendAlertOptions value to be constructed and passed around before it's ever caught — the type itself doesn't prevent it
Because runtime checks are always slower than compile-time checks
Because throwing an error is worse than silently ignoring bad input
Because the SMS client shouldn't contain any validation logic at all
items.explanation: A runtime check can be bypassed, skipped, swallowed by an unrelated try/catch, or simply never reached depending on the code path — as it literally was at Alertly. Illegal-states-unrepresentable means the invalid value can never exist as a value of that type in the first place, which a scattered runtime check doesn't guarantee.
items.reference:
🚫 Illegal state — channel: 'sms' with no phoneNumber
🧱 Made unrepresentable — the type for an sms channel has no shape without a phoneNumber field

Why: a state that can't be constructed can't reach production, no matter how many code paths exist.
items.learnMore: Illegal-states-unrepresentable is a design goal, not a single technique — the most common tool for reaching it in a typed language is a discriminated union (see L2/L3), where each tagged shape only carries the fields valid for that tag. The alternative — a single type with every field optional and a comment saying which combinations are meaningless — leaves the invalid combination fully constructible; every reader and every future contributor has to independently remember the rule the comment states, forever, and Alertly's outage is exactly what happens when one of them doesn't.

items.prompt: What's the key difference between "validating" and "parsing" an input, in the parse-don't-validate sense?
choices: Validating checks the input and returns yes/no while the original loose type continues downstream; parsing converts the input into a new type that proves its own validity
Validating is done at runtime; parsing is only a compile-time concept
Parsing means converting a string to a number; validating means anything else
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
items.explanation: The distinguishing feature isn't when the check runs, it's what happens to the data afterward: validating leaves the same loosely-typed value in play (so every downstream function has to trust or re-check it), while parsing produces a new value of a stricter type that only valid constructions can produce, so nothing downstream needs to re-check.
items.reference:
ValidateParse
Checks, returns bool/throwsConverts to a proving type
Original loose type continuesDownstream only sees the safe type

Why: a type that proves its own validity means nothing downstream has to re-check it.
items.learnMore: Parsing is 'validate once, at the boundary, and encode the result of that validation into the type system so it can never be un-checked again.' Alertly's real bug is a textbook validate-without-parse failure: a check existed somewhere, but the value it checked kept its original loose SendAlertOptions type the whole way through, so every function along the path still had the option (and, eventually, the failure mode) of trusting unchecked data.

items.prompt: In parseAlertRequest(raw), why does converting untyped JSON into an AlertRequest, once, matter more than re-checking the fields inside sendAlert() again?
choices: Because once parseAlertRequest succeeds, the resulting type can only hold valid data — every function after it can trust the type instead of re-inspecting the raw data
Because JSON parsing is always faster than object field access
Because sendAlert() should never contain any logic at all
It doesn't matter — checking twice is always safer than checking once
items.explanation: The whole point of parsing at the boundary is that it needs to happen exactly once — every function downstream of that single parse step receives a type that already proves its own validity, so repeating the check adds redundant code without adding safety the type doesn't already guarantee.
items.reference:

Original loose type continuesDownstream only sees the safe type

Why: a type that proves its own validity means nothing downstream has to re-check it.

items.prompt: sendAlert(id, msg, true, false) is a call to a function with two boolean parameters. What's the specific problem this demonstrates?
choices: At the call site, it's impossible to tell which boolean is which without checking the function signature separately — and any nonsensical combination (both true, both false) is silently accepted
Boolean values are slower to compare than string values at runtime
The function has too many total parameters, regardless of their type
JavaScript doesn't support boolean parameters reliably
items.explanation: This is the boolean-parameter trap: unlabeled positional booleans are unreadable at the call site (which is isUrgent, which is isSilent?) and, worse, the signature doesn't stop combinations that make no sense together — an object literal with named fields, or a union type, both fix the readability and can fix the nonsensical-combination problem.
items.reference:
sendAlert(id, msg, true, false)

Which flag is which? A reader has to open the function signature to find out — and nothing stops true, true even if that combination is meaningless.

Why: unlabeled booleans trade readability and safety for a few characters of brevity.
items.learnMore: The fix is rarely 'remove all booleans' — it's naming them at the call site (named/object parameters) and, where two booleans interact meaningfully, replacing the pair with a small union that only allows the combinations that make sense (e.g. Urgency = {kind:'immediate'} | {kind:'scheduled', sendAt} instead of isUrgent: boolean plus an optional scheduledFor). A boolean is the right tool when the two states are genuinely independent and every combination is valid; it's the wrong tool the moment some combinations aren't.

items.prompt: Why is isUrgent: boolean combined with an optional scheduledFor: Date, on the same request, a boolean-trap-shaped problem even though isUrgent itself is just one flag?
choices: Because the two fields can be set in a combination that contradicts itself (urgent, but also scheduled for later) and nothing in the type stops that
Because Date objects are not allowed to appear in API request types
Because isUrgent should always default to true
Because optional fields are never allowed alongside booleans
items.explanation: The trap isn't limited to two literal boolean parameters — any pair of fields (boolean or optional) whose combination can be nonsensical has the same shape: the type permits a state (urgent AND scheduled-for-later) that the domain doesn't actually allow, and the signature does nothing to prevent it.
items.reference:
sendAlert(id, msg, true, false)

Which flag is which? A reader has to open the function signature to find out — and nothing stops true, true even if that combination is meaningless.

Why: unlabeled booleans trade readability and safety for a few characters of brevity.
items.learnMore: The fix is rarely 'remove all booleans' — it's naming them at the call site (named/object parameters) and, where two booleans interact meaningfully, replacing the pair with a small union that only allows the combinations that make sense (e.g. Urgency = {kind:'immediate'} | {kind:'scheduled', sendAt} instead of isUrgent: boolean plus an optional scheduledFor). A boolean is the right tool when the two states are genuinely independent and every combination is valid; it's the wrong tool the moment some combinations aren't.

items.prompt: A function takes channel: string instead of channel: "email" | "sms" | "push". What specifically does this cost?
choices: A typo like channel: "sm" compiles cleanly and only fails (if ever) at runtime, instead of being caught immediately by the type checker
The function becomes slower because strings take more memory than enums
Nothing — a string can hold any of those three values just as well as a union type can
It only matters if the function is exported from a library
items.explanation: A bare string type accepts any string at all, so a typo, an unsupported value, or a value from an entirely different vocabulary all type-check identically to a correct value — the type system simply isn't asked to help here. A union of literal strings makes the same typo a compile error instead.
items.reference:
channel: string accepts "sms", "sm" (typo), and "telegram" (unsupported) identically.
channel: "email"|"sms"|"push" rejects the last two at compile time.

Why: a bare string type opts out of the compiler's help entirely.
items.learnMore: "Stringly-typed" describes using a general-purpose string where a closed, known vocabulary actually exists. It's tempting because it feels flexible (any code can pass any string) — but that flexibility is exactly the surface area a caller can get wrong. A literal-string union, an enum, or a discriminated union all convert an open-ended string into a closed, checkable set — pick a discriminated union specifically when different values of the field also imply different required data alongside them, the way channel does here.

items.prompt: Why is channel: "email" | "sms" | "push" alone (without also making emailAddress/phoneNumber/deviceToken required per-branch) still not a full fix for Alertly's bug?
choices: Because it fixes typos in the channel value itself, but doesn't stop channel: "sms" from being paired with a missing phoneNumber — that requires a discriminated union tying the field to the tag
Because literal string unions aren't supported in TypeScript
Because it makes the function slower to call
It is a full fix — no further change is needed
items.explanation: A literal-string union narrows which channel values are legal, but on its own it doesn't connect that value to which other fields must be present — that connection is what a discriminated union (tag plus tag-specific fields in one type) adds, which is why L2/L3 go one step further than a plain string union.
items.reference:
channel: string accepts "sms", "sm" (typo), and "telegram" (unsupported) identically.
channel: "email"|"sms"|"push" rejects the last two at compile time.

Why: a bare string type opts out of the compiler's help entirely.
items.learnMore: "Stringly-typed" describes using a general-purpose string where a closed, known vocabulary actually exists. It's tempting because it feels flexible (any code can pass any string) — but that flexibility is exactly the surface area a caller can get wrong. A literal-string union, an enum, or a discriminated union all convert an open-ended string into a closed, checkable set — pick a discriminated union specifically when different values of the field also imply different required data alongside them, the way channel does here.

items.prompt: Why does "minimal surface area" matter for API misuse specifically, not just code cleanliness?
choices: Every additional optional parameter or method roughly multiplies the number of combinations a caller could pass, most of which the author never actually tested
Smaller APIs always run faster than larger ones
It only matters for public libraries, not internal functions
It means removing all parameters and hardcoding behavior instead
items.explanation: Each optional parameter or exposed method is another axis of variation a caller can combine with every other one — most of that combinatorial space is untested and unintended by the author, so a smaller, more deliberate surface directly shrinks the space in which a caller can go wrong.
items.reference:
1️⃣ 1 optional flag → 2 combinations
4️⃣ 4 optional flags → 16 combinations
🎯 Most of those combinations were never intended or tested

Why: surface area and misuse-surface grow together.
items.learnMore: Minimal surface area is about exposing the fewest knobs that solve the actual, current problem — not the fewest knobs period, and not preemptively hiding things a caller genuinely needs. The Alertly interactives demo in this unit makes the combinatorial growth concrete: n optional/boolean fields imply up to 2^n combinations, almost all of which nobody designed for or tested, while a closed, tagged design keeps the number of *valid* states fixed regardless of how the internals grow.

items.prompt: SendAlertOptions exposes emailAddress, phoneNumber, AND deviceToken on every call, regardless of channel. What would a minimal-surface-area redesign change about this specifically?
choices: Only the field relevant to the chosen channel would be reachable at all — the other two wouldn't exist as options a caller could even see for that call
It would rename the three fields to shorter names
It would merge all three fields into a single free-text string field
It would make all three fields required on every call instead of optional
items.explanation: Minimal surface area doesn't mean fewer total fields across the whole API — it means each call site only exposes the options that are actually relevant to it. A discriminated union does exactly this: choosing kind: 'sms' makes phoneNumber the only field available for that branch, not a smaller list of still-optional fields.

items.prompt: "Fail fast at the boundary" means:
choices: Reject invalid input immediately and loudly at the edge of the system, rather than letting it travel inward where the failure is harder to trace back to its cause
Make every function return as quickly as possible regardless of correctness
Retry a failed operation as many times as possible before giving up
Log every function call for debugging purposes
items.explanation: "Fail fast" is about where and how quickly a problem surfaces, not about performance — catching bad input at the boundary means the failure happens close to its cause (this request, this field), rather than three layers deep where it's much harder to trace back to the original bad call.
items.reference:
🚪 Boundary: reject immediately, loudly, close to the cause
🕳️ Deep in the stack: swallowed by unrelated error handling

Why: distance from the cause is what makes a bug hard to trace.
items.learnMore: The value of failing fast isn't 'failing' — it's the location. Alertly's check existed but ran deep inside code written for a different purpose (retrying flaky SMS sends), where an unrelated try/catch could absorb its failure. Moving the same logical check to the boundary — the moment external input first enters the system — removes every intervening layer that could accidentally intercept it, which is why 'at the boundary' is the load-bearing part of the phrase, not just 'fast'.

items.prompt: Alertly's actual check for a missing phoneNumber existed, but ran inside the SMS-sending code, several layers past where the request was first received. What does "fail fast at the boundary" say should have been different?
choices: The check itself was fine in principle, but its location was wrong — it needed to run at the point where the request first entered the system, not deep inside a function written for a different purpose
The check should have been removed entirely
The check should have retried the SMS send instead of throwing
Nothing — the check's location doesn't matter as long as it exists somewhere
items.explanation: This is the specific lesson from L2's diagnosis: the check's logic was correct, but by the time it ran, it was inside code wrapped by a broad try/catch meant for a different failure mode. Moving the same check to the boundary means it runs before that unrelated catch block exists anywhere in the path.
items.reference:
🚪 Boundary: reject immediately, loudly, close to the cause
🕳️ Deep in the stack: swallowed by unrelated error handling

Why: distance from the cause is what makes a bug hard to trace.

Alertly's check existed but ran deep inside code written for a different purpose (retrying flaky SMS sends), where an unrelated try/catch could absorb its failure. Moving the same logical check to the boundary — the moment external input first enters the system — removes every intervening layer that could accidentally intercept it, which is why 'at the boundary' is the load-bearing part of the phrase, not just 'fast'.

items.prompt: How does a discriminated union make an invalid field combination impossible, mechanically — not just "harder"?
choices: Each tagged shape in the union only has field slots for the data valid for that tag — there is no field slot in the 'sms' shape for a value to be missing from, because that shape was never constructable without it
The union runs a validation function automatically before every use
TypeScript deletes any object that doesn't match at runtime
It relies on developers remembering to check the tag before using a field
items.explanation: The mechanism is structural, not procedural: {kind:'sms', phoneNumber: string} simply has no representation for 'sms with no phoneNumber' — there's no field to leave empty. Compare this to an object with phoneNumber as an always-optional field, which does have a representation for that missing case.
items.reference:
ShapeCan phoneNumber be missing?
{kind:'sms', phoneNumber?: string}Yes — a valid value of this type
{kind:'sms', phoneNumber: string}No — not a valid value of this type

Why: removing a field's optionality removes a representable state, not just adds a check.
items.learnMore: A discriminated union is a sum type: a value of the union type is exactly one of its member shapes, never a blend of two, and the tag field is what the compiler uses to narrow which shape it's looking at inside a switch or if-chain. This is structurally different from an enum-plus-optional-fields design, where the tag restricts one field's possible values but leaves every other field's optionality independent of the tag — which is precisely the gap that let channel: 'sms' and phoneNumber: undefined coexist in Alertly's original type.

items.prompt: Inside a switch (channel.kind) { case "sms": ... } block, TypeScript lets you access channel.phoneNumber without a non-null assertion (!). Why?
choices: Because the compiler has narrowed the type of channel to exactly the 'sms' member of the union inside that branch, which is the only member that has a phoneNumber field
Because TypeScript assumes all fields exist unless told otherwise
Because switch statements disable type checking inside their branches
Because phoneNumber was declared as a global variable
items.explanation: This is called narrowing: once the compiler sees channel.kind === "sms" is true in that branch, it knows channel can only be the union member tagged 'sms', and that member's type definition is the only one it needs to check field access against — which is exactly why phoneNumber is guaranteed present there, no assertion needed.

Why: removing a field's optionality removes a representable state, not just adds a check.

This is structurally different from an enum-plus-optional-fields design, where the tag restricts one field's possible values but leaves every other field's optionality independent of the tag — which is precisely the gap that let channel: 'sms' and phoneNumber: undefined coexist in Alertly's original type.

items.prompt: Why does the redesigned AlertChannel type prevent someone from writing { kind: "sms", deviceToken: "abc" } (the exact bug from Alertly's outage)?
choices: Because the 'sms' member of the union is defined as { kind: "sms"; phoneNumber: string } — it has no deviceToken field, so an object literal with deviceToken doesn't match any member of the union and fails to type-check
Because deviceToken is a reserved keyword in TypeScript
Because the compiler runs the object through a validation function automatically
It doesn't fully prevent it — a runtime check is still required
items.explanation: TypeScript checks an object literal for excess/mismatched properties against the union member it's structurally closest to — since kind: "sms" only matches the { kind: "sms"; phoneNumber: string } member, an object with deviceToken instead of phoneNumber doesn't satisfy that member and the whole literal fails to compile, exactly as shown in L3's @ts-expect-error example.

items.prompt: The principle of least astonishment, applied to API design, means:
choices: A call's behavior should match what its name and shape suggest, with no hidden side effects a reader wouldn't expect from reading the signature alone
An API should surprise its users occasionally to keep documentation interesting
Every function should have exactly one parameter
Functions should never throw exceptions, only return error codes
items.explanation: Least astonishment is about the gap between what a signature implies and what the code actually does — a function called sendAlert that silently no-ops on certain inputs, instead of throwing or documenting that behavior prominently, violates the principle even though its name is otherwise accurate.
items.reference:
✅ Expected: sendAlert either sends or throws
😲 Astonishing: sendAlert silently does nothing on some inputs

Why: a reader shouldn't need to read the implementation to know what a call does.
items.learnMore: Least astonishment is a design heuristic borrowed from broader interface design (physical products included) — the more a call's actual behavior diverges from what a reasonable reader would guess from its name/signature/types, the more that gap becomes a source of bugs, because callers act on the guess rather than the reality. In Alertly's case, the astonishing part wasn't sendAlert's happy path — it was the silent no-op on an invalid channel/field combination, a behavior no caller reading the function name would predict.

items.prompt: sendAlert() silently swallowed the missing-phoneNumber error via a broad try/catch written for a different purpose. Which principle does this most directly violate?
choices: Least astonishment — a function named sendAlert that neither sends the alert nor tells the caller it failed does something no reasonable reader would predict from its name
DRY — the code repeats itself unnecessarily
Single responsibility — the function does too many unrelated things
Encapsulation — internal details are exposed to the caller
items.explanation: The violation here is specifically about the gap between expectation and behavior: a caller reading `sendAlert(options)` reasonably expects either the alert to go out or an error to surface — silently doing neither is the astonishing part, distinct from the other named design principles listed as distractors.
items.reference:
✅ Expected: sendAlert either sends or throws
😲 Astonishing: sendAlert silently does nothing on some inputs

Why: a reader shouldn't need to read the implementation to know what a call does.

In Alertly's case, the astonishing part wasn't sendAlert's happy path — it was the silent no-op on an invalid channel/field combination, a behavior no caller reading the function name would predict.

items.prompt: A constructor/factory that takes 8 optional parameters (all with defaults) is convenient to call with just 1-2 arguments. What's the trade-off L2's checklist points at?
choices: Convenience at the call site is bought by leaving the space of possible constructed objects huge and mostly untested, since any subset of the 8 can be combined
Optional parameters always run slower than required ones
There is no trade-off — more optional parameters is strictly better design
It only matters if the constructor is called more than once
items.explanation: Every one of the 8 optional parameters can be present or absent independently, so the constructor can produce up to 2^8 = 256 different shapes of the resulting object — almost none of which the author individually reasoned about or tested, even though each individual call looks simple.
items.reference:
😌 Convenient: new Alert({message: 'x'})
🧨 Also legal: new Alert({message:'x', channel:'sms', deviceToken:'y'})

Why: convenience for the easy case and safety for every case pull in opposite directions.
items.learnMore: The 'optional-everything constructor' pattern is common because it's genuinely convenient for the simplest call — but the convenience doesn't shrink the space of what the constructor can actually produce, it just hides that space at the easiest call site. The fix isn't necessarily 'make everything required' (that just moves the pain to every caller); it's usually splitting the constructor into a small number of named, self-consistent factory functions or union variants, each of which is fully valid on its own — the same discriminated-union move used throughout this unit.

items.prompt: What's a more targeted fix than "make every constructor parameter required" for the optional-everything constructor trap?
choices: Split the single do-everything constructor into a small number of named factory functions (or union variants), each of which only accepts the fields valid for that specific case
Remove all parameters and hardcode a single default object
Add a comment listing which combinations are valid
Convert every parameter to a string so any combination compiles
items.explanation: Making everything required doesn't fix the underlying issue — it usually just pushes every caller to pass placeholder values for fields irrelevant to their case. Splitting into targeted factories (createEmailAlert(...), createSmsAlert(...), or a union constructed via a parse/smart-constructor function) keeps each one minimal and self-consistent instead.
items.reference:
😌 Convenient: new Alert({message: 'x'})
🧨 Also legal: new Alert({message:'x', channel:'sms', deviceToken:'y'})

Why: convenience for the easy case and safety for every case pull in opposite directions.
items.learnMore: The 'optional-everything constructor' pattern is common because it's genuinely convenient for the simplest call — but the convenience doesn't shrink the space of what the constructor can actually produce, it just hides that space at the easiest call site. The fix isn't necessarily 'make everything required' (that just moves the pain to every caller); it's usually splitting the constructor into a small number of named, self-consistent factory functions or union variants, each of which is fully valid on its own — the same discriminated-union move used throughout this unit.

items.prompt: According to L2's diagram, what are the three places an invalid combination like channel: 'sms' with no phoneNumber can end up being caught (or not)?
choices: Compile time (if unrepresentable in the type), runtime (if a check exists and isn't bypassed/swallowed), or production (if no check exists or the runtime check gets swallowed)
Only ever at runtime, regardless of how the type is designed
Only during code review, if a human happens to notice it
Only in a staging environment, never in production
items.explanation: The diagram's point is that these three outcomes correspond to three different design choices, not to luck: making the state unrepresentable guarantees compile time; a runtime check merely might catch it (as Alertly's case showed, it can be swallowed); and no check at all guarantees the worst outcome, production.
items.reference:
🟢 Compile time — unrepresentable in the type
🟡 Runtime — a check exists, if it isn't bypassed
🔴 Production — no check, or the check gets swallowed

Why: earlier and more guaranteed is strictly better, when it's available.
items.learnMore: The reason this progression matters isn't just 'earlier is better' in the abstract — each stage is strictly more expensive and less certain than the one before it. A compile error is caught before a human even sees the code merged. A runtime check depends on the code path actually reaching it and nothing intercepting the failure (Alertly's try/catch is the counterexample). A production failure depends on someone noticing at all, and by then the cost has already been paid — in Alertly's case, 45 minutes of an unpaged outage.

items.prompt: Why is "caught at compile time" strictly more reliable than "caught by a runtime check," even when the runtime check's logic is written correctly?
choices: A compile-time check can't be skipped, bypassed, or accidentally swallowed by unrelated code — it runs on every build, unconditionally, before the code can even be merged or deployed
Compile-time checks run faster than runtime checks
Runtime checks are always written incorrectly
There's no real difference in reliability, only in when the error message appears
items.explanation: A correctly-written runtime check still depends on the code path actually reaching it at the moment of execution, with nothing else (like an unrelated try/catch) intercepting its failure — exactly the gap Alertly's outage exposed. A compile-time check has no equivalent 'did it actually run this time' dependency.
items.reference:
🟢 Compile time — unrepresentable in the type
🟡 Runtime — a check exists, if it isn't bypassed
🔴 Production — no check, or the check gets swallowed

Why: earlier and more guaranteed is strictly better, when it's available.
items.learnMore: The reason this progression matters isn't just 'earlier is better' in the abstract — each stage is strictly more expensive and less certain than the one before it. A compile error is caught before a human even sees the code merged. A runtime check depends on the code path actually reaching it and nothing intercepting the failure (Alertly's try/catch is the counterexample). A production failure depends on someone noticing at all, and by then the cost has already been paid — in Alertly's case, 45 minutes of an unpaged outage.

items.prompt: In parseAlertRequest(raw), what does the function do if the raw JSON's channel.kind is "sms" but phoneNumber is missing?
choices: Throws an InvalidAlertRequestError immediately, before any AlertRequest or AlertChannel value is ever constructed from that input
Silently defaults phoneNumber to an empty string
Constructs the AlertChannel anyway and lets sendAlert() figure it out later
Logs a warning and continues with channel set to 'push' instead
items.explanation: This is the whole point of a parsing boundary function: it either succeeds and returns a value of the safe, proven type, or it fails loudly right there — it never partially constructs an invalid value and lets it continue downstream, which is exactly the failure mode Alertly's original code had.

✅ Success → a fully-valid AlertRequest, nothing downstream re-checks it
❌ Failure → throws immediately, no partial value escapes

items.prompt: L2 says the trade-off between a permissive and a constrained API isn't automatically worth making in every case. What's the deciding factor it points to?
choices: The blast radius and risk profile of the API — a public library or a production alerting path is worth the extra ceremony far more than a script three people use once
Whichever version has fewer total lines of code
Whichever version the original author personally prefers
Always prefer the constrained version, with no exceptions
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames this as a judgment call tied to who's calling the API and what's at stake if a call goes wrong — an internal helper used by code you fully control has a very different risk profile than a public, widely-depended-on interface, which is why 'always constrain everything maximally' isn't the actual lesson.
items.reference:
Low stakesHigh stakes
3-person internal scriptPublic library, live alerting path
Permissive is often fineConstrained earns its ceremony
items.learnMore: This trade-off is the reason 'illegal states unrepresentable' isn't presented as a rule to apply uniformly everywhere — the ceremony of a discriminated union plus a parsing boundary is real cost (more types to define, more up-front thought about every valid shape), and that cost is worth paying in proportion to how expensive being wrong is. Alertly's alerting path pages humans during live outages, which is about as high-stakes as an internal API gets; a one-off data migration script run once by its own author has a much smaller blast radius if it's wrong.

items.prompt: A teammate argues every internal function, no matter how small or low-stakes, should use full discriminated-union parsing boundaries "because it's strictly safer." What's the strongest counterpoint from this unit?
choices: It is safer, but the ceremony has a real cost too — applying it uniformly regardless of actual risk means paying that cost even where the blast radius of a mistake is tiny and would be caught immediately anyway
Discriminated unions are only available in TypeScript, so the advice doesn't generalize
Safety and ceremony are unrelated, so there's no trade-off to weigh at all
Runtime checks are always safer than compile-time checks, so the teammate is simply wrong
items.explanation: The unit's stance isn't 'safety is bad' — it's that safety has a cost (definitional ceremony, more up-front modeling work) that should be matched to the actual risk, not applied uniformly as a rule of thumb regardless of what's at stake if a given piece of code is wrong.

items.prompt: Implement parseChannel(raw) so it accepts an object like {kind, phoneNumber, emailAddress, deviceToken} and returns a plain object {kind: 'sms', phoneNumber} ONLY if raw.kind === 'sms' and raw.phoneNumber is a non-empty string. If phoneNumber is missing or not a string, throw an Error (any message). This mirrors the exact bug from the unit: the sms channel must never be constructible without a phone number.

rejects sms with an empty string phoneNumber

items.explanation: This is a smart constructor: the only way to get a { kind: 'sms', ... } value out of this function is to supply a valid phoneNumber. Every caller downstream of parseChannel can trust that any value tagged 'sms' has a real phone number, without re-checking — the check ran exactly once, at construction, instead of being something every consumer has to remember to redo.

items.prompt: Implement parseUrgency(raw). If raw is undefined or raw.kind === 'immediate', return { kind: 'immediate' }. If raw.kind === 'scheduled', it must also carry a non-empty string raw.sendAt — return { kind: 'scheduled', sendAt: raw.sendAt }. Any other shape (including a raw that tries to claim BOTH immediate and scheduled at once, e.g. {kind:'immediate', sendAt:'2026-01-01'}) must throw an Error — sendAt is only valid alongside kind:'scheduled'.
items.explanation: This closes the second boolean-trap gap named in L1/L2: isUrgent and scheduledFor used to be two independent optional fields that could both be set, which is nonsensical (urgent, but also scheduled for later?). Modeling urgency as a union means 'immediate' and 'scheduled' are mutually exclusive by construction — there is no field slot for a value to be both at once.
items.reference:
⚡ {kind:'immediate'} — no sendAt field exists on this shape
🕒 {kind:'scheduled', sendAt} — sendAt only exists here

Why: mutual exclusivity by construction, not by convention.
items.learnMore: Booleans and optional fields that only make sense in certain combinations are a recurring shape of this same bug — isUrgent: boolean plus an optional scheduledFor: Date is structurally identical to the channel/phoneNumber problem, just with two fields instead of a tag and a value. The fix is the same move: a union with two tagged shapes, each carrying exactly the field relevant to it, so 'urgent and scheduled' simply has no representation.

items.prompt: The permissive createUser(name, isAdmin, isModerator, isBanned) allows nonsensical combinations (banned admins, both isAdmin and isModerator at once). Implement createUser(name, role) where role must be exactly one of 'member', 'moderator', or 'admin' (a string), and return { name, role }. If role is anything else, throw an Error. This collapses 3 independent booleans (8 combinations, most nonsensical) into 1 field with exactly 3 valid values.

tests.description: rejects a banned-and-admin style combination that the old boolean signature would have allowed

items.explanation: 3 independent booleans imply up to 2^3 = 8 combinations, most of which (banned admin, admin-and-moderator) were never intended. Replacing them with a single role field closed to exactly 3 valid values shrinks the space of representable states from 8 mostly-invalid ones down to exactly 3, all valid — this is minimal surface area applied concretely, not just as a slogan.
items.reference:
🧨 3 booleans → 8 combinations, most invalid
✅ 1 role field → exactly 3 valid states

Why: collapsing independent flags into one closed field removes the invalid combinations entirely.
items.learnMore: This is the same combinatorial-growth idea as this unit's interactive demo: n independent boolean/optional fields imply up to 2^n representable combinations, and only a fixed, usually much smaller number of those are ever actually meaningful. Collapsing related flags into a single closed field (a string union, an enum, or a tagged union when different values also need different associated data) is the most direct way to shrink that gap back down to exactly the valid states and nothing else.

items.prompt: Implement parseAge(raw). It must return raw as a number if raw is a positive integer (greater than 0). Otherwise it must throw an Error. Unlike a plain isValidAge(raw) that returns true/false, this function's return value itself IS the proof the age is valid — that's the parse-don't-validate distinction from L2.
items.explanation: A validate-only version (isValidAge(raw): boolean) would still leave callers holding the original, unchecked raw value even after calling it — nothing stops someone from ignoring the boolean and using raw anyway. parseAge instead only ever returns a number when it's already been proven positive and integer — any caller holding the return value has, by construction, a valid age, with no separate boolean to remember to check.
items.reference:
isValidAge(raw)parseAge(raw)
Returns true/falseReturns a proven-valid number, or throws
raw is still around, uncheckedOnly the checked value survives
items.learnMore: This is the smallest possible demonstration of parse-don't-validate: a validating function reports on the data but leaves the data itself unchanged and just as untrustworthy as before the call; a parsing function converts the data into a form whose very existence is the proof of validity. The pattern scales from a single primitive like age up to full object graphs like AlertRequest — the mechanism (throw immediately, return only the validated shape) doesn't change with size.

items.prompt: Implement makeDiscount(type, value). If type === 'percentage', value must be a number strictly between 0 and 100 (exclusive) — return { type, value }. If type === 'fixed', value must be a positive number — return { type, value }. Any other type, or a value outside the allowed range for that type, must throw an Error. This prevents illegal states like a 150% discount or a -$5 fixed discount.
items.explanation: A permissive { type: string, value: number } discount type can represent { type: 'percentage', value: 150 } perfectly legally — nothing about the shape says a percentage can't exceed 100. makeDiscount is a smart constructor: because it's the only sanctioned way to build a discount, and it enforces the range per-type before returning, a 150% discount or a negative fixed discount can never exist as a constructed Discount value anywhere downstream.
items.reference:
🚫 {type:'percentage', value:150} — never gets constructed
✅ {type:'percentage', value:20} — the only kind of value that exists

Why: range checks belong at construction, not scattered wherever a discount is later used.
items.learnMore: This generalizes illegal-states-unrepresentable beyond "which fields exist" (like AlertChannel) to "which values a field can legally hold given another field" (percentage vs. fixed have different valid ranges for the same value field). A smart constructor is the right tool either way — the invariant lives in exactly one place (the constructor), instead of being re-derived by every piece of code that later reads a Discount and hopes it's sane.

items.prompt: Implement createShippingLabel(kind, details). If kind === 'domestic', details must have a non-empty string zipCode — return { kind: 'domestic', zipCode: details.zipCode }. If kind === 'international', details must have a non-empty string country AND a positive number customsFee — return { kind: 'international', country: details.country, customsFee: details.customsFee }. Any other kind, or missing required details, must throw an Error.
items.explanation: This is a factory/smart-constructor doing the same work as parseChannel: each kind of label carries exactly the fields that kind needs (a domestic label has no customsFee field to leave unset; an international one has no way to exist without both country and customsFee), so a mismatched label — international with no customs fee, domestic with a country instead of a zip — is never constructed in the first place, not just rejected somewhere downstream.
items.reference:
🏠 domestic → only needs zipCode
🌍 international → needs country AND customsFee

Why: a factory that branches per kind keeps each branch's required fields separate and enforced.
items.learnMore: This is the same shape as AlertChannel/parseChannel applied to a shipping domain: a fixed, small number of valid label kinds, each with its own required fields, built through a single factory that's the only way to construct one. The number of valid states stays fixed (2 here) no matter how the underlying details grow — which is exactly what this unit's interactives.json demo contrasts against a permissive design's exponentially growing combination space.
